name: UGC NET Paper 1
fullName: UGC National Eligibility Test – Paper 1 (General Paper on Teaching & Research Aptitude)
conductingBody: National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission
frequency: Twice a year (June and December cycles)
approxCandidates: ≈7–11 lakh registrations per cycle (2024–26). Paper 1 is common to all 80+ subjects.
eligibility: Master's degree (or final year) with 55% (50% for OBC-NCL/SC/ST/PwD/third gender), or a 4-year UG degree with 75%. JRF upper age limit is 30 years (with relaxations). No upper age limit for Assistant Professor or PhD admission.

notification.summary: NTA released the UGC-NET December 2026 information bulletin on 8 Oct 2026. Online applications are open until 28 Oct 2026, and the CBT is scheduled for 14–19 Dec 2026. In the previous June 2026 cycle, results for 84 subjects were declared by late August 2026, with more than 4,000 candidates qualifying for JRF. Fresh exams were held on 9–10 Sep 2026 for English, Commerce and Sociology after errors were found in those papers. Dates come from the bulletin and news reports via web search; the ugcnet.nta.nic.in portal itself could not be reached from the research sandbox.

pattern.notes: In the real exam, Paper 1 (50 Q, 100 marks) and Paper 2 (100 Q, 200 marks) are taken together in one 3-hour sitting with no break. Each question carries 2 marks and there is no negative marking. The 60 minutes shown here is a suggested allocation for Paper 1. Officially the 50 questions are spread over 10 units, typically about 5 each. Comprehension is usually one passage with 5 questions, and Data Interpretation is a table or chart with 5 questions. The question bank holds 60 original questions (6 per unit) for building mocks. Qualification falls into three categories: JRF + Assistant Professor + PhD, Assistant Professor + PhD, and PhD only.

trendAnalysis.summary: This analysis covers June 2024 (re-conducted as a CBT in Aug–Sep 2024), Dec 2024 (held Jan 2025), June 2025, Dec 2025 and June 2026. Paper 1 is consistently rated easy to moderate. Comprehension, DI, ICT and Higher Education are the most scoring units, while Logical Reasoning (Indian logic: pramanas and hetvabhasas, plus syllogisms) and Research Aptitude are the most time-consuming. Recent shifts include more NEP 2020, SWAYAM and Academic Bank of Credits questions in Higher Education, more matching and assertion–reason items, and chronology-based questions. Environment questions increasingly focus on SDGs, COP and India's net-zero commitments. The DI set is usually one table of 5–6 rows needing percentage or ratio calculations.

topics.topic: Methods of Teaching & Online Platforms (SWAYAM, MOOCs)

resources.notes: During each answer-key challenge window, NTA publishes the shift-wise question papers with provisional keys and candidates' recorded responses on the UGC NET portal (also reachable as ugcnet.nta.ac.in). Final answer keys are published with the result. Older papers (2012–2018, from the CBSE/NTA era) were archived on ugcnetonline.in. Coaching sites host compilations, which are not official.

questions.question: The 'reflective level' of teaching, in which learners engage in problem-centred, critical thinking, is mainly associated with:
questions.explanation: The levels of teaching are memory (Herbart), understanding (Morrison) and reflective (Bigge and Hunt). The reflective level is the highest and is problem-centred.

questions.topic: Methods of Teaching & Online Platforms (SWAYAM, MOOCs)
questions.question: Which Government of India platform hosts MOOCs offered by Indian universities and national coordinators such as NPTEL, UGC and CEC?
questions.explanation: SWAYAM is India's national MOOC platform. Shodhganga is a thesis repository, and Vidwan and IRINS are databases of experts and research profiles.

questions.question: Evaluation carried out during the course of instruction to monitor learning and give feedback is called:
questions.explanation: Formative evaluation is ongoing and improves learning while it is happening. Summative evaluation judges achievement at the end.

questions.question: The term 'andragogy', popularised by Malcolm Knowles, refers to:
options: Teaching by peers of the same age
The art and science of helping adults learn
questions.explanation: Knowles contrasted andragogy (adult learning, which is self-directed and experience-based) with pedagogy (child learning).

questions.topic: Methods of Teaching & Online Platforms (SWAYAM, MOOCs)
questions.question: Which of the following is a learner-centred method of teaching?
options: Recitation of notes by the teacher
questions.explanation: In the project method, learners plan and carry out purposeful activities themselves. The other three are teacher-centred.

questions.question: In the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), which is the highest level of the cognitive domain?
questions.explanation: The revised order is Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. 'Create' replaced 'Synthesis' and became the top level.

questions.question: Research undertaken by practitioners to solve an immediate problem in their own setting, such as a teacher improving attendance in her class, is called:
questions.explanation: Action research is practical, problem-focused and conducted by practitioners for immediate improvement.

questions.question: A researcher compares the Class V scores of children who did and did not attend pre-school. Pre-school attendance has already happened and is not manipulated. This design is:
questions.explanation: When the independent variable has already occurred and cannot be manipulated, the design is ex post facto (causal-comparative).

questions.question: Which of the following is a probability sampling technique?
questions.explanation: In stratified random sampling every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection. The other three are non-probability techniques.

questions.question: Rejecting a null hypothesis when it is actually true is known as:
questions.explanation: A Type I error (α) is a false rejection of a true null hypothesis. A Type II error (β) is failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

questions.question: In APA style, an in-text citation normally includes:
options: The author's surname and the year of publication
The full title of the work and its page count
questions.explanation: APA uses the author–date format, for example (Sharma, 2024). Footnote numbering belongs to styles such as Chicago notes.

questions.question: Under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, similarity up to what level is treated as 'Level 0' and attracts no penalty?
questions.explanation: The levels are: up to 10% = Level 0 (minor, no penalty), 10–40% = Level 1, 40–60% = Level 2, and above 60% = Level 3.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"For most of human history, knowledge travelled by word of mouth. Epics, genealogies and medicinal recipes were preserved not in libraries but in memory, recited by trained specialists who treated accuracy as a sacred duty. Scholars once dismissed such oral traditions as unreliable, assuming that every retelling must distort the original. Field studies in the twentieth century challenged this view. Researchers found that some communities transmitted long texts across centuries with remarkable fidelity, using rhythm, repetition and strict teacher–student lineages as safeguards. At the same time, oral cultures were never frozen: storytellers adapted episodes to their audiences, adding local heroes or contemporary jokes while keeping the core intact. Writing, when it arrived, did not simply replace memory; it changed what people thought worth remembering. Once a text could be consulted on a shelf, the effort of memorisation seemed wasteful, and the specialist reciter slowly lost his social standing. Today, as digital search makes even written reference instant, some educators worry that a similar shift is under way – not the loss of knowledge itself, but the loss of the habit of holding knowledge within oneself."

Earlier scholars dismissed oral traditions as unreliable because they assumed that:
options: Writing had existed before oral traditions
Oral texts were too short to be useful
Every retelling must distort the original
questions.explanation: The passage says scholars dismissed oral traditions 'assuming that every retelling must distort the original'.

Which is the most suitable title for the passage?

questions.explanation: The passage traces how oral memory, writing and now digital search have changed attitudes to remembering.

questions.question: The study of body movements, gestures and facial expressions as a form of communication is called:
questions.explanation: Kinesics is body language. Proxemics concerns the use of space, chronemics the use of time, and haptics touch.

questions.question: A 'semantic barrier' to communication arises mainly from:
options: Different interpretations of words and symbols
Loud physical noise in the surroundings
questions.explanation: Semantic barriers are problems of meaning, such as ambiguous words, jargon and poor translation. The other options are physical, organisational and psychological barriers.

questions.question: Effective classroom communication is best described as:
options: Communication that avoids questions from students
One-way transmission from teacher to students
Interactive and two-way, with feedback from learners
questions.explanation: Feedback and interaction make communication effective and confirm that the message has been understood.

questions.question: Which model of communication first introduced 'noise' as an element that distorts the message between transmitter and receiver?
questions.explanation: Shannon and Weaver's 1949 mathematical model added a noise source in the channel. The Aristotle, Lasswell and Berlo models do not include noise.

questions.question: The agenda-setting theory of mass media holds that the media:
options: Reflect public priorities without shaping them
Influence which issues the public considers important
Have no measurable effect on audiences
Tell people exactly what opinions to hold
questions.explanation: McCombs and Shaw argued that the media may not tell people what to think, but they strongly influence what people think about.

questions.question: The 'grapevine' in an organisation refers to:
options: The informal network of communication among members
questions.explanation: The grapevine is the informal, unofficial communication channel that runs alongside formal channels.

questions.question: Find the next number in the series: 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is (previous × 2) + 1, so 63 × 2 + 1 = 127.

questions.question: Find the next letter in the series: B, E, I, N, ?
questions.explanation: The positions are B = 2, E = 5, I = 9, N = 14, with gaps +3, +4, +5, so the next gap is +6: 14 + 6 = 20 = T.

questions.question: If MOUSE is written as NPVTF in a certain code, how will CHAIR be written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward (M→N, O→P, …). So C→D, H→I, A→B, I→J, R→S, giving DIBJS.

questions.question: Pointing to a man, Riya says, "He is the only son of my mother's father's only daughter." How is the man related to Riya?
questions.explanation: Her mother's father's only daughter is Riya's mother. The only son of Riya's mother is Riya's brother.

questions.question: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost price and then allows a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: Take CP = 100. Then MP = 140 and SP = 140 × 0.85 = 119, so the profit is 19%.

questions.question: What is the compound interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually?
How many pramanas (valid means of knowledge) are accepted in the Nyaya school of Indian philosophy?
questions.explanation: Nyaya accepts four pramanas: pratyaksha, anumana, upamana and shabda. Bhatta Mimamsa and Advaita accept six, Buddhists two, and Sankhya three.

questions.question: "Devadatta is getting fatter, yet he does not eat during the day; therefore he must eat at night." Which pramana does this knowledge illustrate?
questions.explanation: Arthapatti postulates a fact (eating at night) that is needed to explain an otherwise inexplicable situation. This is the classic 'fat Devadatta' example.

questions.question: In Nyaya logic, a fallacious reason (a defective middle term) is called:
questions.explanation: Hetvabhasa means 'that which appears to be a reason but is not'. Pratijna (thesis), udaharana (example) and nigamana (conclusion) are members of the five-membered syllogism.

questions.question: In the traditional square of opposition, two propositions that cannot both be true but can both be false are called:
questions.explanation: A and E propositions are contraries: they cannot both be true but may both be false. Contradictories cannot both be true or both be false, and subcontraries cannot both be false.

questions.question:
Statements: All pens are books. Some books are bags.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are bags. II. Some bags are books.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: 'Some books are bags' converts to 'Some bags are books', so II follows. The bags that are books need not include any pens, so I does not follow.

questions.question: An argument in which the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion is called:
questions.explanation: Deductive validity means it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Inductive arguments only make the conclusion probable.

questions.question: Data collected first-hand by a researcher through a questionnaire survey is known as:
questions.explanation: Primary data is collected directly by the investigator for the study at hand. Secondary data comes from existing sources.

questions.question: In the context of the internet, 'URL' stands for:
questions.explanation: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a resource on the web.

questions.question: When an e-mail is sent with some addresses in the 'BCC' field:
options: Those recipients' addresses are not visible to the other recipients
Those recipients receive the e-mail at a lower priority
Attachments are removed for those recipients
questions.explanation: BCC (blind carbon copy) hides those recipients' addresses from everyone else on the message.

questions.question: Shodhganga, maintained by INFLIBNET, is a repository of:
questions.explanation: Shodhganga is the INFLIBNET reservoir of theses and dissertations submitted to Indian universities.

questions.question: Which of the following is a volatile memory that loses its contents when power is switched off?
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile. ROM, hard disks and flash memory are non-volatile.

questions.question: SWAYAM Prabha is:
options: A national digital library of e-books
A scholarship portal for research scholars
A group of DTH channels that telecast educational programmes round the clock
questions.explanation: SWAYAM Prabha is the Ministry of Education's set of DTH channels broadcasting curriculum-based educational content 24×7.

questions.question: The Government of India's UMANG app, which provides access to many government services on one platform, stands for:
options: Unified Mechanism for Administrative and National Governance
Union Mobile App for Network Governance
Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance
Universal Mobile Access for National Governance
questions.explanation: UMANG stands for Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance, an initiative of MeitY and NeGD.

questions.question: How many Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted under the UN 2030 Agenda?
questions.explanation: There are 17 SDGs with 169 targets. The earlier Millennium Development Goals numbered 8.

questions.question: The Montreal Protocol (1987) deals with:
options: Binding greenhouse-gas emission cuts for developed countries
Protecting the ozone layer by phasing out ozone-depleting substances
questions.explanation: Montreal addresses ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs. The other options describe the Kyoto Protocol, the CBD and the Basel Convention.

questions.question: PM2.5 refers to airborne particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of:
questions.explanation: PM2.5 means fine particles of 2.5 µm or less. Such particles can penetrate deep into the lungs.

questions.question: Under the 'Panchamrit' commitments announced at COP26 (Glasgow), India aims to achieve net-zero emissions by:
questions.explanation: India announced a net-zero target year of 2070 at COP26 in 2021.

questions.question: The magnitude (energy released) of an earthquake is commonly expressed on the:
questions.explanation: Richter (and moment magnitude) scales measure magnitude. The Mercalli scale measures intensity (observed effects), Beaufort measures wind and Saffir–Simpson hurricanes.

questions.question: In which year was the Environment (Protection) Act enacted in India?
questions.explanation: The EP Act was enacted in 1986 after the Bhopal gas tragedy. 1972 is the Wildlife Protection Act, 1974 the Water Act and 1981 the Air Act.

questions.question: The ancient centre of learning Takshashila (Taxila) is located in present-day:
questions.explanation: Taxila is near Rawalpindi in Pakistan. Nalanda and Vikramashila were in Bihar, and Valabhi was in Gujarat.

questions.question: NEP 2020 aims to raise the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in higher education, including vocational education, to:
questions.explanation: NEP 2020 targets a higher-education GER of 50% by 2035, up from about 26.3% in 2018.

questions.question: Which single umbrella regulator for higher education (excluding medical and legal education) is proposed under NEP 2020?
options: All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE)
questions.explanation: NEP 2020 proposes HECI, with four verticals: NHERC, NAC, HEGC and GEC.

questions.question: The University Education Commission (1948–49) was chaired by:
questions.explanation: The Radhakrishnan Commission (1948–49) dealt with university education. Kothari chaired the Education Commission (1964–66), Mudaliar the Secondary Education Commission (1952–53), and Yash Pal the 2009 committee.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution lists the Fundamental Duties, including the duty to protect the natural environment?
questions.explanation: Article 51A lists the Fundamental Duties, and clause (g) covers protecting the environment. Article 48A is a Directive Principle on the environment, 21A covers the right to education, and 45 early childhood care.

questions.question: The Academic Bank of Credits (ABC) introduced under NEP 2020 is meant to:
options: Digitally store the academic credits earned by students and enable multiple entry and exit
questions.explanation: ABC is a digital credit repository. It allows credit accumulation and transfer, which supports multiple entry and exit.
